---
title: Call a tool
description: tool.invoke calls a tool the way an agent would, with the cursor and confirmation. Use it for a "Try it" button, a keyboard shortcut, an onboarding tour or a test.
sidebar:
  label: 6. Call a tool
---

Every tool has one verb, **`invoke`**. It calls the tool the way an agent would, through the page's WebMCP: the cursor
moves, fields are typed, confirmation applies, and you get the answer the agent would get. Use it for a "Try it"
button, a keyboard shortcut, a guided tour or an end-to-end test.

## A complete example

A tool called from a button. Where `invoke` comes from depends on how the tool was written:

<View title="Vite">

<Tabs syncKey="tool-api" hash={false}>
<Tab title="useWebTool">

The hook returns `invoke` for the tool it registers, the same function on every render.

```tsx
const addToCart = useWebTool({
  id: "add_to_cart",
  // …
});

<Button
  variant="outline"
  onClick={() => addToCart.invoke({ size: "M", quantity: 2 })}
>
  Show me
</Button>
```

</Tab>
<Tab title="defineWebTool">

A defined tool has `invoke` on it: import the tool and call it.

`invoke` resolves to what `execute` returned, typed: for `get_cart`, `{ lines, total }`.

It works only while the tool is on: a component's tool while the component is mounted, a defined tool while its
`match` fits.

## What it resolves and rejects with

- **It resolves to what `execute` returned**, or `undefined` when the call navigated the page away. The common tools'
  readers return MCP results, `{ content, structuredContent }`.
- **It rejects with a [`WebToolError`](/reference/core/web-tool-error)** carrying the code an agent would have read:
  `invalid_input` for input that fails the schema, `unavailable` for a confirmation with nothing to click, `failed`
  when `execute` throws, and the others in [Errors](/concepts/errors). It also rejects when the tool is not on the page
  right now.
- **A confirm-gated tool waits** for the person's click, like an agent's call. Pass a `signal` to stop waiting:
  `invoke(input, { signal })` rejects with an `AbortError` when it aborts.

For a unit test, use `run` instead: it validates and executes with no page, no cursor and no confirmation.

```ts
const orders = await listOrders.run(
  { limit: 1 },
  { signal: new AbortController().signal, source: "test" },
);
```

## From the console

In development, the devtools put the same call on `window.agent`, by name:

```js
await agent.invoke("get_cart");
await agent.list();
```

End-to-end tests drive tools the same way: the example apps' Playwright tests call `window.agent.invoke`.

## Try it

Render `<CartSummary />` and click **Check the cart**: it shows "Lines: 1, total $28.00". Then, in the console, call the tool
by name:

```js
await agent.invoke("get_cart");
```

## Options you'll use most

| `invoke(input, options)` | What it is for |
|---|---|
| `input` | The tool's parameters, typed by its schema. Optional when it takes none. |
| `options.signal` | Abort the call, including a wait for the person's click. |

Reference: [`defineWebTool`](/reference/core/define-web-tool) (the `WebTool` it returns, with `invoke` and `run`) and
[`useWebTool`](/reference/react/use-web-tool) (what the hook returns).
